passage: Rekha, don't laugh, but I skipped the Bihu husori on our street tonight. Everyone's out with the dhol, and I'm at my desk with the physics mock. I got rank one last time, and Sir said in front of the whole class, "Bhupen is our topper." When he said that, I felt real. Like I counted. So if I come second now, what am I? I keep a chart on my wall, every test, every rank, in red pen. Ma says I look tired. I told her tired is fine, second is not. Sometimes I think I don't even like physics. I like being first. Is that strange? Anyway, I'll dance next year, after the boards. Maybe.

qa.q: What does Bhupen keep on the wall?
qa.a: A chart of every test and every rank, in red pen.

qa.q: What is Bhupen afraid of about coming second?
qa.a: He feels anxious that without the top rank he would not count, since being called the topper is what made him feel real and worthy.

qa.q: What could help Bhupen keep the effort without losing all rest?
qa.a: Join part of the Bihu evening, set fixed breaks, and look for something he enjoys in physics itself, not only in the rank.

qa.q: How might Ma see Bhupen's late nights?
qa.a: Ma sees that he looks tired and is likely worried that the chase for rank leaves him no room to rest or enjoy the festival.

grounding: A teenager skips a festival to guard a top rank, feeling his worth depends on results.

23 December, hostel, 11 pm
Filed my nomination for student council president today, right before everyone leaves for the Christmas break. My hands were shaking when I signed.
Why am I doing this? Honestly, two reasons. One: the girls' hostel curfew is ridiculous and nobody fights it properly. I can. Two: I loved it when the whole canteen went quiet during my debate speech. I want that. I want people to listen when I talk.
Tonight I made a list of who would be on my team. Then I noticed I had crossed out Akash, not because he's bad, but because he argues with me. That felt ugly. A council of people who agree with me isn't leadership, it's a fan club. Adding him back. Chandrika, remember why you started.

qa.q: What position did Chandrika file a nomination for?
qa.a: Student council president.

qa.q: Why did crossing out Akash feel ugly to Chandrika?
qa.a: Chandrika felt uneasy and ashamed on noticing the wish for influence sliding into control, cutting Akash only because he disagrees.

qa.q: What small check could help Chandrika stay on the serving side of power?
qa.a: Keep people who disagree on the team, as Chandrika did with Akash, and keep asking whether each decision serves the group or only the wish to be listened to.

qa.q: What would change for the council if Akash stayed off the list?
qa.a: It would lose someone who questions and argues, turning into a fan club that agrees with Chandrika instead of testing ideas.

grounding: A young adult stands for student leadership, wanting both to help and to be listened to, and catches a slide toward control.

Karthigai Deepam fell on the night before Jaya's anatomy viva, and her hostel in Hyderabad banned open flames. At home in Madurai, Amma and Paati would be lining every step and wall with little clay lamps by six.
Jaya had carried five lamps from home, wrapped in newspaper. At seven she asked the warden, twice, until she got ten minutes on the terrace with a bucket of water beside her.
"You're really doing this before the viva?" Lavanya asked, eyebrows up. "It's just oil and wicks."
"It's the one night the whole family does the same thing at the same time," Jaya said, striking the match. "Wherever we are."
The five flames steadied in the wind. Jaya felt her shoulders loosen for the first time all week. Lavanya was quiet, then crouched and shielded the last lamp with her hand.

qa.q: How many lamps had Jaya carried from home?
qa.a: Five lamps, wrapped in newspaper.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel once the five flames steadied?
qa.a: She felt calm and connected, her shoulders loosening for the first time all week, sharing the ritual with her family from far away.

qa.q: How did Jaya keep the tradition while respecting the hostel rule?
qa.a: She asked the warden for permission, used only ten minutes on the terrace and kept a bucket of water ready, honouring both the ritual and the rule.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's view have changed during the ten minutes?
qa.a: Lavanya began doubtful, calling it just oil and wicks, but by shielding the last lamp she seemed to understand why it mattered to Jaya.

grounding: A young adult keeps a festival lamp ritual in a hostel before a viva, finding belonging in it despite a doubting roommate.

On Khichdi day the smoke of a hundred small fires drifted over Bahraich, and Raghav sat on the ghat steps with Yogesh, bowls of hot khichdi between them.
"Last chance," Yogesh said. "The jaggery business. Partners. We could be big in two years."
Raghav looked at his new ID card from the district cooperative office, still stiff in its plastic. A fixed salary, a pension, Maa's medicines paid every month without counting, his sister's school fees safe.
"I can't, yaar," he said. "Not now."
He felt the calm of that decision, like a roof over the house. And under it, a small worry: what if Yogesh really did become big, and he spent forty years stamping the same forms?
Yogesh nudged him. "Okay. But I'm sending you the first batch free."

qa.q: Where was Raghav's new ID card from?
qa.a: The district cooperative office.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Raghav have after saying no to Yogesh?
qa.a: He feels calm, like a roof over the house, knowing his family is secure, and also a small worry about missing out and stamping the same forms for forty years.

qa.q: What might help Raghav live with the choice?
qa.a: Remind himself why security matters so much right now, stay close to Yogesh's venture as a friend, and revisit the question if circumstances change.

qa.q: How does Yogesh seem to take Raghav's refusal?
qa.a: Yogesh takes it warmly, nudging him and promising the first batch free, which suggests the friendship matters more than the deal.

grounding: A young professional chooses a steady job over a friend's venture to keep his family secure, feeling both calm and worry.

Counselling note, Thursday. Sudha
Dolma came in for the third time about the Bengaluru offer. Today was different. She had drawn three columns on a page: Freedom, Security, Family ways. "I keep wanting all three to win," she said. "They can't, not every time."
She said that for this choice, freedom ranks first: the design job is the work she has wanted since school. Security second, since the job is steady enough. Family ways third, for now, and she was clear it hurt to say so. She will still go home for Losar every year.
When I asked about her mother, who wants her to take the state job in Gangtok, she said, "Amala ranks them differently. That's not wrong. It's hers."
Next step: she will talk to her mother on Sunday, page in hand.

qa.q: What three columns did Dolma draw?
qa.a: Freedom, Security, Family ways.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel ranking family ways third?
qa.a: Dolma felt clear about the choice but pained, saying it hurt to put family ways third, even for now.

qa.q: Why does naming a ranking for this one choice help?
qa.a: It stops Dolma waiting for all three values to win; she can decide about Bengaluru, still keep Losar at home, and revisit the order for later choices.

qa.q: How might Dolma's mother see the Bengaluru choice?
qa.a: Her mother, who wants her in the Gangtok state job, likely ranks security and family ways higher and may feel worried, though Dolma plans to talk it through with her on Sunday.

grounding: An adult ranks freedom, security and family ways for one job choice and respects her mother's different ranking.

"Nirmala, can I use your pencil? Mine broke," Jeevan whispered. The Ganpati drawing had to be finished before the bell.
"What will you give me?"
"Huh?"
"I'll lend my pencil if you lend your eraser. The one that smells like strawberry."
"But I need it too!"
"Then no pencil." Nirmala pulled it close. "That's fair. You get something, I get something."
"You're not even using an eraser now!"
"I might. Deal or no deal?"
Jeevan sighed and pushed the eraser across. "Deal. But I want it back after one line."
"Two lines."
"One and a half."
Nirmala grinned and handed over the pencil. "Deal."

qa.q: What did Nirmala ask for in return for the pencil?
qa.a: Jeevan's eraser, the one that smells like strawberry.

qa.q: What does Nirmala think makes the deal fair?
qa.a: Nirmala feels sure and a bit pleased with the bargain, believing fair means each person gets something, rather than thinking about Jeevan's broken pencil and Jeevan's need.

qa.q: How could a teacher build on Nirmala's sense of fairness?
qa.a: Accept that fair trades matter to Nirmala, and also ask how Jeevan feels with a broken pencil and the bell coming, so Nirmala notices Jeevan's need as well as the deal.

qa.q: How does Jeevan feel about the trade?
qa.a: Jeevan feels frustrated, protesting that Nirmala isn't even using an eraser, but agrees because the drawing must be finished before the bell.

grounding: A child lends a pencil only in exchange for an eraser, seeing fairness as a trade.

On Vishwakarma Puja the Kolkata sky was full of kites, and Irawati had lent Harsha her best one, the red fighter with the long tail, because his had torn. Harsha flew it straight into the neighbour's coconut tree and left it there.
The next afternoon Harsha came up to the terrace with a brand-new blue kite. Irawati waited. He didn't offer it. He didn't even say sorry.
"Can I fly yours for a bit?" she asked.
"It's new. Maybe tomorrow."
Irawati's face went hot. She marched downstairs and told her Baba, "I'm never lending him anything again. Never. I gave him my best one and he gives me nothing."

qa.q: Where did Harsha fly Irawati's red kite?
qa.a: Straight into the neighbour's coconut tree.

qa.q: Why does Irawati say she will never lend Harsha anything again?
qa.a: She feels cheated and angry, because she gave her best kite and Harsha gave nothing back, not even a sorry.

qa.q: How could Baba help Irawati after this?
qa.a: Listen to how unfair it felt, then help her think about telling Harsha directly how she feels, rather than only swearing never to share.

qa.q: How might Harsha see the afternoon?
qa.a: Harsha may simply be thinking of his new kite and not realise how much the lost red one mattered to Irawati.

grounding: A child who lent her best kite and got nothing back feels cheated and vows never to lend again.

The week before Christmas, Class 4 at the Andheri school was making cards, and Joseph Sir walked between the benches with a box of glitter. At the back, Anirban was guarding his twenty-four colour pencils with both arms.
"Tashi has none," Joseph Sir said quietly. Tashi had joined only on Monday.
"He can use them if he gives me his sticker sheet," Anirban said. "That's fair."
Joseph Sir crouched. "It is fair, in a way. You like things to be even. Can I ask you something? If you were new and had nothing, and everyone wanted a sticker first, how would you feel?"
Anirban looked at Tashi, who was colouring a star with a blunt pencil. "Bad, I think."
He slid the box to the middle of the bench.

qa.q: How many colour pencils did Anirban have?
qa.a: Twenty-four.

qa.q: What did Anirban feel on looking at Tashi colouring with a blunt pencil?
qa.a: He felt a pang of sympathy, answering "Bad, I think," as he imagined being new and having nothing.

qa.q: What did Joseph Sir do well without shaming Anirban?
qa.a: He agreed the deal was fair in a way, then asked Anirban to imagine being new, turning his attention from the trade to Tashi's feelings.

qa.q: How might Tashi feel when the box slides to the middle of the bench?
qa.a: Tashi, new since Monday and colouring with a blunt pencil, would likely feel welcomed and relieved.

grounding: A teacher respects a child's sense of fair trade while asking him to imagine a new classmate's feelings.

passage:
Two days before Lunar New Year, the Vancouver apartment smelled of dumpling dough, and Mina had a plan written on an index card.
"Dad," she said, laying it next to the flour. "Proposal. I do the dishes every night, take out the recycling, and clean the bathroom on Saturdays. In exchange, I get a phone. Not a fancy one."
Chen raised an eyebrow, still pleating a dumpling. "And if I say we do chores because we live here together?"
"Then I'd still do them," Mina said quickly. "Probably. But this way it's fair. You get a clean bathroom, I get a phone. Everybody wins."
She had even drawn a little table with two columns: My job. My payment.
Chen laughed despite himself. "You've turned our home into a shop."
"A very fair shop," Mina said.

qa.q: What was Mina's plan written on?
qa.a: An index card.

qa.q: How does Mina feel about her proposal?
qa.a: She feels confident and a bit proud of it, sure it is fair because each side gets something, like a shop.

qa.q: How could Chen respond so Mina sees chores as more than a price?
qa.a: Take the honest offer seriously, then talk about how the family shares work because they care for each other, perhaps deciding about the phone separately from the chores.

qa.q: How does Chen see the deal?
qa.a: Chen finds it funny, laughing that she has turned the home into a shop, while hinting that chores are about living together, not payment.

grounding: A teenager offers a list of chores in exchange for a phone, treating family duty as a price.
